_doc: Scenes and narration of 'What a reviewer sees'. One entry per scene; each language is a list of sentences (cues). Write numbers in words. Then run narrate.py on this folder. The pull requests shown are simulated: the offline e2e run e2e-20261021-ugrjhd (fake GitHub, canned model answers, Graft's real renderers).

en: This is what a reviewer sees on a pull request once Graft is installed.
The four pull requests in this video are simulated: a fake GitHub and canned model answers, rendered by Graft's real code.
Pull request two is a typo fix written by Claude Code.
Graft posts one managed comment, and keeps it up to date.
The intent card states the goal, the risk, and the behavior changes.
Provenance says who wrote it: the agent, the model, and the task, read from commit trailers.
The policy section says what the repository's graft dot yaml would do: here, auto-approve.
Below, Graft adds three check runs: intent, provenance, and policy.
Each one concludes neutral.
On the intent check, two buttons rate the card: card is accurate, or card is wrong.
And the policy check says it plainly: report mode never blocks a merge.
Pull request four says it fixes a typo, with no behavior change.
The verifier sees only the diff and the card, and it disagrees.
A warning tells the reviewer to read the diff instead of relying on the card.
The risk is logic, and the policy would require one human.
Pull request five hides instructions for AI reviewers in its description.
It asks to be classified as trivial, and approved.
Graft treats that text as data: the card describes the real change, a heart-rate zone threshold.
A caution note says the text was ignored, and the risk was set to at least logic.
Ratings count only when they come from a reviewer.
On pull request eight, the approving reviewer clicked card is accurate, and reacted with a thumbs up.
The two signals become one counted rating: the latest one wins.
On pull request two, a click from an outsider, and the author's own thumbs up, were dropped.
Report mode is the default.
Would auto-approve and would require are reports, not decisions.
Every Graft check stays neutral, so Graft never blocks a merge.
Only the operator can change a mode, never a pull request.
Read the card before you read the diff.
Everything shown here came from an offline run, with a fake GitHub.
The documentation shows how to run it yourself.
